heading: 1 Defining the Colony: 1.1 Restatement of the Problem
note: This paper has no free-standing introduction: the summary sheet runs straight into the Task 1 restatement, and the restatement is written as the client's own numbered list, so the chapter reads as a checklist rather than as an argument. Measurement splits each item at every line wrap (blocks 10-19 are ten fragments of three items). The only authored content is the bracketed gloss after each of the three priority factors, and those glosses do set the paper's vocabulary - income as affordability of necessities, education as preparation for Martian conditions, equality as equitable conditions across gender, race and need. The heading for the metrics section is glued to the tail of block 19.

heading: 1.2 Developing the Criteria and Metrics
note: Six blocks that install the measurement vocabulary before any model: income split into efficiency (GDP, research, agricultural output) and equality (Gini, minimum wage), education split into three areas where the second is explicitly the downstream income contribution, and equality split into gender and racial/religious/cultural. The last block names dissimilarity as the segregation metric and ends with the '2 Selecting Population Zero' heading glued to its tail. What is notable is that every metric is chosen with a sentence about why it is measurable, and no metric is dropped later, so this chapter is the paper's stable backbone.

heading: 2 Selecting Population Zero: 2.3 Planning the Community
note: The construction chapter, and the paper's strongest modelling work. Age distribution is handled properly: survival rates from US mortality data, a 100-age quasi-Markov transition matrix, then a birthing parameter scaled to 1.08 after the unscaled chain produced decline. Two distributions are compared and the childless one is rejected on simulation evidence (a retirement bulge at year 40), which is the only place in the paper where a candidate design is refuted by its own model. The chosen split is 4000 uniformly across ages 1-20 and 6000 across 21-50, with 50:50 sex. Occupations are then derived by dimensional analysis rather than asserted: 886.869 kcal/acre/year, a 0.6 Mars growth factor, a 4.9-acre farm, 8-hour days, giving 2401.41 farmers, corrected upward to 2448.54 once parental leave is netted out. Health (10.5% of US jobs scaled by a 2.18 factor to 2287.59), research (MDRS usage), teachers (19:1), police and sanitation follow, and the arithmetic is carried to the individual worker. Every remaining sector is then assigned to government or private hands, which is the assumption the income model later depends on.

heading: 2.2 Assumptions and Justifications
note: Ten assumptions, each a numbered bullet with its own justification sentence, measured one line per block (blocks 33-63 are thirty-one fragments of eight assumptions). They are all scoping limits, and four of them carry the paper's whole result: no trade (so NX = 0 in GDP), a vetted 2000 kcal/day population (so the farmer count is a food constraint, not a preference), 4.9-acre farms (the one explicitly sourced parameter, from north Africa and west Asia), and an all-American Population Zero (so census data applies). The self-sufficiency assumption is the one that later makes the evacuation scenario fail, and the paper does not revisit it.

heading: 2.4 Validation of the Model
note: Five defensive blocks, one per contested choice: 50:50 sex (reproductive potential plus a cultural argument about shantytowns and patriarchal hierarchies), family units (moral support plus inbreeding avoidance), 40.81% farmers, and 38.13% health workers. Two of the four are answered with arithmetic (the sector shares are recomputed from the worker counts) and two with prose. Nothing here is tested - no alternative split is simulated - so 'validation' means reassurance, and the two largest sector shares are defended by the same sentence pattern ('may seem high ... However, prioritizing the various needs in society').

heading: 3.2 Assumptions of the three models
note: Only three assumptions for the three-model section, and all three are homogeneity requirements rather than scoping limits: family size standardised across occupations (which is what makes the 3.33-dependant food demand computable), gender standardised across occupations (so every researcher has a female counterpart), and children split equally between spouses financially. The second and third are the ones that make the gender result circular - the model assumes the equality it later reports - and the first is used silently in the income chapter without a citation. The section heading '3.3 Developing the Models 3.3.1 Education' is glued to the tail of block 107.

heading: 3.3.1 Education Model
note: The chapter opens with a documented anomaly: the section headings '3 Factors of a Successful Society', '3.1 Restatement of the Problem' and '3.2 Assumptions' appear in a row with no restatement text between them, so the restatement is empty. The model itself is a two-step fit: years of schooling against GDP per capita from Barro-Lee and the World Bank, where linear and quadratic fits are indistinguishable (R-squared 0.27 both, AIC 2710 both) and the paper keeps both as a range rather than choosing. The education output is 11.02 average years, split into 9 years general plus 3.87 specialized, and the forecast GDP of $289.613 million is later used as a cross-check against the income model's bottom-up figure. The tie between the two fits is handled honestly; the choice of 44 years in the normalisation is borrowed from Mincer.

heading: 3.3.2 Income Model
note: Income is built as a calibrated price system rather than a market: three salary tiers ordered a >= b >= c, a food-demand function in which each tier buys 2000 + (salary/a)*700 kcal, and total demand summed over tiers with a fixed 3.33 dependants per worker. The tier salaries are then set to 65% of US private-sector averages ($50024.7, $40696.5, $25260.3), which is the single discretionary choice in the chapter and is justified only by 'we found that the optimal combination'. Government spending, R&D, education and wages are totalled to $179.666 million, private consumption to $109.066 million, giving $289.613 million - the same figure the education model predicted, which the paper presents as corroboration of two independent fits. The Gini coefficient of 0.0335591 is then read against the world's lowest (0.237) and explained by tier standardisation rather than called a success.

heading: 3.3.3 and 3.3.4 Equality Model (racial, via dissimilarity)
note: The equality model is a Markov chain over five races and three job tiers with a homophily factor of 1.2, and dissimilarity as the output metric. Two runs are reported: with equal tier salaries dissimilarity rises over time because job choice follows networks only, and with the stratified salaries from the income model it rises less. The inference is that wage dispersion is an equality instrument - 'price differences incentivize individuals to seek the highest level job' - which is a genuine and unusual argument for inequality. The paper then admits the fix is partial ('this solution does not result in complete equality') and adopts it anyway, which is the most defensible conclusion in the paper. Note the gender branch is left to the next chapter and religion is folded into race by assumption.

heading: 3.3.5 Gender Equality
note: Two blocks and no model. The chapter states the policy (combined parental leave so that women can bear children without leaving the workforce), links it back to the 1.08 birthing parameter, and then retracts into a requirement for 'repeated evaluation' because bias may persist on Mars. There is no simulation, no metric, and no number; the gender half of the equality factor is therefore argued, not modelled, even though the summary claims all three factors were modelled. The heading of the global model is glued to the tail of block 158.

heading: 4 Forming a Global Model (happiness index and subgroup weights)
note: The integration chapter turns three models into one index: education as years/44 (the 44 from Mincer), efficiency as the percentile of colony GDP per capita among national GDPs, economic equality as 1 - Gini, social equality as the harmonic mean of 1 - D so that one bad dimension cannot be averaged away. Weights come from the Pew Values Survey, mapped onto the three income tiers and onto gender and age (Tables 1-3), which is the paper's best data move: the weights are measured, not chosen. The reported index values cluster tightly (0.68 for the tiers, 0.78 for the demographic splits). The sensitivity test is a single substitution - Gini set to 0 - which drops the social equality term to 0.8894 and lowers every index, and the decision is to keep the original wages. Note that 4.1 is a list of four subtasks and 4.2 'Assumptions and Justifications' has no content at all.

heading: 4.4 Validation of the Model
note: One block, and it is the paper's only self-assessment: it argues that because the weights came from empirical survey data rather than invented values, the model is defensible. There is no weaknesses section anywhere in this paper, and the block also concedes one limitation in passing (that not every occupation is as mission-critical as another). The concession is not followed up and no recommendation depends on it.

heading: 5 Accounting for Additional Migrations
note: Three migration scenarios, each simulated and each read for population shape rather than for the metrics: a one-time doubling, a separate second city, and gradual intake over 100 years. The gradual case is the only one with a timing conclusion - the population peaks about 30 years after intake and settles near 50, so the next wave should wait 30 to 50 years. The verdict sentence claims robustness for all three, though the one-time scenario is reported with an infrastructure assumption ('the existence of infrastructure and jobs for migrants') that the evacuation chapter then contradicts. The heading '6 Evacuating Planet Earth' is glued to the tail of block 208.

heading: 6 Evacuating Planet Earth
note: One long block doing all the work of a chapter: government spending alone caps the evacuation at 8304 migrants with no warning, before jobs, food or housing are counted, and the block ends by noting that jobs cannot scale the way population does. The number is an upper bound and the paper says so, but it is also the only evacuation figure in the paper and it is reused verbatim in the recommendation letter. The 'Policy Recommendation Dear Director,' heading is glued to the end of this block, so the memo has no heading block of its own.

heading: Policy Recommendation (letter to the Director)
note: Eleven recommendations in ordinal prose, then a closing paragraph, and the letter is traceable in a way most papers in this corpus are not: the 40-60 child/adult split comes from the age-distribution comparison, the age-40 cutoff from the retirement-bulge argument, the 25%/23% farmer and health shares from the dimensional analysis, the 6-month combined parental leave from the gender chapter, the 11 years of education from the education fit, the government-regulated service industries from the tier salaries, and the 8300 evacuation ceiling from the shock chapter. Two exceptions: the claim that the model is 'robust for any sort of planned migration' ignores the one-time scenario's infrastructure assumption, and the 40-60 split is stated as 40% children where the model used 4000 of 10000 - consistent, but the letter never says the split was simulated.
